```{python}
#| label: setup
import sys, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, "../slides")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

from plotstyle import setup, CL
plt = setup()

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_predict

core = pd.read_parquet("../data/spine/core.parquet").drop(columns=["flag"])
c5 = pd.read_parquet("../data/spine/angle_c_country.parquet").drop(columns=["flag"])

OUT, TRT = "digital_intensity", "has_ai_strategy"
CTRL = ["gdp_pc_eur", "population", "employment_ths", "productivity_idx",
        "gfcf_meur", "cloud_use", "ict_specialists", "time"]

d = (core.merge(c5, on=["geo", "time"])
         .dropna(subset=[OUT, TRT] + CTRL).reset_index(drop=True))
Xr = d[CTRL].to_numpy(float)
Dr = d[TRT].to_numpy(float)
Yr = d[OUT].to_numpy(float)
NAIVE = Yr[Dr == 1].mean() - Yr[Dr == 0].mean()
```

# {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

::: {style="margin-top: 1.2em"}
### You have a superb predictive model. Why can you still not use it to choose a policy? {style="color:#F7F6F3"}
:::

## Outline

| | |
|---|---|
| **1** | Where we are, and what this adds |
| **2** | The setup, and what identification requires |
| **3** | Why the naive plug-in fails |
| **4** | Fix 1 — Neyman orthogonality |
| **5** | Fix 2 — cross-fitting |
| **6** | Heterogeneous effects |
| **7** | What this does *not* fix |

## Learning objectives

::: {.tight}
- State the partially linear model and name the **nuisance functions**
- Decompose the naive estimator's error into **regularisation** and **overfitting** bias
- Explain why an orthogonal score turns two slow rates into one fast enough one
- Implement cross-fitting, and say precisely which bias it removes
- Report a heterogeneous effect **without** doing undisclosed multiple testing
:::

# 1 · What this adds {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Sessions 05–09 gave you prediction

| Session | What you can now do |
|---|---|
| **05** | fit well with more predictors than rows |
| **06–07** | classify, and fit arbitrary non-linear surfaces |
| **08–09** | compress and cluster without an outcome at all |

::: {.warn}
And none of it answers the only question a minister ever asks: **if we do this, what happens?**
:::

## The gap, made concrete

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.7, 2.9))
lab = ["no AI strategy", "has AI strategy"]

ax = axes[0]
for k, c in [(0, CL.muted), (1, CL.accent)]:
    ax.hist(d.loc[Dr == k, "gdp_pc_eur"] / 1000, bins=22, alpha=.68, color=c, label=lab[k])
ax.set_xlabel("GDP per capita  (thousand €)"); ax.set_ylabel("country-years")
ax.legend(fontsize=7.5)

ax = axes[1]
sh = d.groupby("time")[TRT].mean()
ax.plot(sh.index, sh.to_numpy() * 100, "o-", color=CL.accent, lw=2.4, ms=4)
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("% of countries with a strategy")
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
Countries that adopt AI strategies are **richer**, and they adopt **later**. Treatment is not
random, and no amount of predictive accuracy repairs that.
:::

## The number this produces

```{python}
#| echo: true
print(f"mean digital intensity, has strategy : {Yr[Dr==1].mean():6.2f}")
print(f"mean digital intensity, no strategy  : {Yr[Dr==0].mean():6.2f}")
print(f"naive difference in means            : {NAIVE:+6.2f} points")
```

::: {.warn}
Ten points. If you publish that as the effect of adopting a national AI strategy, you have published
the difference between rich and poor countries wearing a policy label.
:::

## What today adds

> A way to use the flexible learners of Sessions 05–07 for the **nuisance** parts of a causal
> question, while keeping the **valid confidence interval** of Session 03.

::: {.check}
This is the reconciliation of the two halves of the course. Everything before Session 05 had honest
inference and rigid functional form; everything after had flexible fit and no inference. Today they
meet.
:::

# 2 · The setup {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The partially linear model

$$Y = \theta_0 D + g_0(X) + U, \qquad \mathbb{E}[U \mid X, D] = 0$$
$$D = m_0(X) + V, \qquad \mathbb{E}[V \mid X] = 0$$

::: {.step}
$\theta_0$ is what you want. $g_0$ and $m_0$ are **nuisance functions** — you do not care about them,
but you cannot avoid them.
:::

::: {.check}
Classical econometrics assumes $g_0$ is linear. DML's premise is that you would rather estimate it
flexibly — because **functional-form error in $g_0$ contaminates $\theta_0$**.
:::

## Identification requires three things

::: {.tight}
1. **Conditional ignorability** — $\{Y(1), Y(0)\} \perp D \mid X$
2. **Overlap** — $0 < P(D = 1 \mid X) < 1$ almost surely
3. **SUTVA** — no interference between units, one version of treatment
:::

::: {.warn}
No amount of machine learning substitutes for these. They are assumptions **about the world**,
defended with institutional knowledge — not with cross-validation.
:::

## Check overlap before anything else

```{python}
ps = cross_val_predict(
    RandomForestClassifier(300, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
    Xr, Dr, cv=5, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
bad = ((ps < .05) | (ps > .95)).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 26)
ax.hist(ps[Dr == 0], bins=bins, alpha=.72, color=CL.muted, label="no strategy")
ax.hist(ps[Dr == 1], bins=bins, alpha=.72, color=CL.accent, label="has strategy")
for b in (.05, .95):
    ax.axvline(b, color=CL.warn, ls="--", lw=1.6)
ax.text(.5, ax.get_ylim()[1] * .82, f"{bad:.0%} of observations lie outside [0.05, 0.95]",
        ha="center", color=CL.warn, fontsize=9, fontweight="600")
ax.set_xlabel(r"estimated propensity  $\hat m(X) = \hat P(D=1 \mid X)$")
ax.set_ylabel("country-years"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
Two in five observations have almost no counterpart in the other arm. For those countries the data
contain **no comparison**, and any estimate is extrapolation.
:::

# 3 · Why the naive plug-in fails {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The obvious thing to do, and why it breaks

Estimate $\hat g_0$ with a lasso or a forest on the full sample, then regress $Y - \hat g_0(X)$ on
$D$. Decomposing the error:

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta - \theta_0) = \underbrace{a}_{\to\,N(0,\Sigma)}
+ \underbrace{b}_{\text{regularisation bias}} + \underbrace{c}_{\text{overfitting bias}}$$

::: {.tight}
- **$b$** scales like $\sqrt n \times \|\hat g_0 - g_0\|$. ML estimators converge **slower** than
  $n^{-1/2}$ — that is the price of flexibility — so $b$ **diverges**
- **$c$** arises because $\hat g_0$ was fitted on the same observations where it is evaluated
:::

::: {.warn}
Two distinct problems. Two distinct fixes.
:::

## Watch it happen, with $\theta_0$ known

```{python}
#| echo: true
THETA = 0.5

def simulate(n=300, p=20, seed=0):
    """Partially linear model with a genuinely non-linear g0 and m0."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
    g = np.exp(X[:, 0]) / (1 + np.exp(X[:, 0])) + 0.25 * np.cos(X[:, 1]) * X[:, 2]
    m = 0.8 * X[:, 0] + 0.25 * np.sin(X[:, 1])
    D = m + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    Y = THETA * D + g + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    return X, D, Y

def forest():
    return RandomForestRegressor(60, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)

def estimate(X, D, Y, mode):
    n = len(Y)
    if mode == "naive":                       # regress Y - ghat(X) on D
        return (D @ (Y - forest().fit(X, Y).predict(X))) / (D @ D)
    if mode == "orthogonal":                  # residualise BOTH, same sample
        ty = Y - forest().fit(X, Y).predict(X)
        td = D - forest().fit(X, D).predict(X)
    else:                                     # residualise BOTH, cross-fitted
        ty, td = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
        for tr, te in KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1).split(X):
            ty[te] = Y[te] - forest().fit(X[tr], Y[tr]).predict(X[te])
            td[te] = D[te] - forest().fit(X[tr], D[tr]).predict(X[te])
    return (td @ ty) / (td @ td)
```

## Fifty replications, three estimators

```{python}
REPS = 50
res = {m: np.array([estimate(*simulate(seed=s), m) for s in range(REPS)])
       for m in ("naive", "orthogonal", "cross-fitted")}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 3.0))
for (nm, v), c in zip(res.items(), [CL.warn, CL.muted, CL.good]):
    ax.hist(v, bins=18, alpha=.68, color=c,
            label=f"{nm}:  bias {v.mean()-THETA:+.3f}")
ax.axvline(THETA, color=CL.ink, lw=2.2)
ax.text(THETA + .006, ax.get_ylim()[1] * .88, r"true $\theta_0 = 0.5$",
        color=CL.ink, fontsize=9, fontweight="600")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\hat\theta$"); ax.set_ylabel("replications")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
The naive estimator misses by **more than half the true effect**, and its spread is *narrow* — it is
confidently wrong. A tight confidence interval around it would be worse than no estimate.
:::

# 4 · Fix 1 — orthogonality {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Use a different score

$$\psi(W;\theta,\eta) = \big(Y - \ell_0(X) - \theta(D - m_0(X))\big)\big(D - m_0(X)\big)$$

with $\eta = (\ell_0, m_0)$, $\ell_0(X) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]$, $m_0(X) = \mathbb{E}[D \mid X]$.
Solving $\mathbb{E}[\psi] = 0$:

$$\theta_0 = \frac{\mathbb{E}\big[(Y-\ell_0(X))(D-m_0(X))\big]}{\mathbb{E}\big[(D-m_0(X))^2\big]}
= \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(\tilde Y, \tilde D)}{\mathrm{Var}(\tilde D)}$$

::: {.check}
That is **exactly Frisch–Waugh–Lovell** from Session 02: regress residualised $Y$ on residualised
$D$. The only change is that the residualising is done by a forest instead of a projection matrix.
:::

## What "orthogonal" means

The directional derivative of $\mathbb{E}[\psi]$ with respect to the nuisance, at the truth, is
**zero**:

$$\partial_\eta\,\mathbb{E}\big[\psi(W;\theta_0,\eta_0)\big]\big[\eta - \eta_0\big] = 0$$

::: {.step}
So a small error in $\hat\eta$ has only a **second-order** effect on $\hat\theta$. The bias term
becomes

$$\sqrt n \times \|\hat\ell - \ell_0\| \times \|\hat m - m_0\|$$
:::

## Two slow rates multiply into a fast one

```{python}
n = np.logspace(2, 5, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.95))
slow = n ** (-0.25)
ax.loglog(n, slow, color=CL.warn, lw=2.4)
ax.loglog(n, slow ** 2, color=CL.good, lw=2.6)
ax.loglog(n, n ** (-0.5), color=CL.ink, ls="--", lw=1.6)
ax.text(1.3e2, slow[10] * 1.25, r"each nuisance:  $n^{-1/4}$", color=CL.warn,
        fontsize=9, fontweight="600")
ax.text(1.3e2, slow[10] ** 2 * .42, r"their product:  $n^{-1/2}$", color=CL.good,
        fontsize=9, fontweight="600")
ax.text(2.2e4, 4e-3, r"parametric rate", color=CL.ink, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("sample size  n"); ax.set_ylabel("estimation error")
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
Neither nuisance need converge at $n^{-1/2}$. Each need only beat $n^{-1/4}$ — a rate lasso, forests
and boosting achieve under reasonable conditions. **Two slow rates multiply into one fast enough
rate.** That is why it is called *double*.
:::

# 5 · Fix 2 — cross-fitting {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The remaining bias, and the split that removes it

::: {.step}
Term $c$ exists because $\hat\ell$ and $\hat m$ were fitted using the very observations at which
they are then evaluated. That correlates the estimated nuisance with the residual.
:::

::: {.check}
The fix is the one you already know from Session 04: **never evaluate a fit on data it was fitted
on**. Here it is applied to the nuisance step.
:::

## The procedure, drawn

```{python}
K = 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 2.9))
for k in range(K):
    for j in range(K):
        col = CL.warn if j == k else CL.accent
        ax.barh(K - 1 - k, 1, left=j, height=.62, color=col,
                alpha=1.0 if j == k else .55, edgecolor=CL.bg, linewidth=2)
    ax.text(-.25, K - 1 - k, f"round {k+1}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5)
ax.text(K + .2, K - 1, "fit  $\\hat\\ell, \\hat m$  here", color=CL.accent,
        fontsize=9, va="center", fontweight="600")
ax.text(K + .2, K - 2, "form residuals here", color=CL.warn,
        fontsize=9, va="center", fontweight="600")
ax.set_xlim(-1.9, K + 4.6); ax.set_ylim(-.6, K - .3)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(K) + .5); ax.set_xticklabels([f"fold {j+1}" for j in range(K)],
                                                     fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(visible=False)
for s in ("left", "bottom"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.muted}
Every observation gets a residual, and no observation's residual used a nuisance fitted on itself.
:::

## Then pool, and get a standard error

$$\hat\theta = \frac{\sum_i \tilde Y_i \tilde D_i}{\sum_i \tilde D_i^2}, \qquad
\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{\frac1n\sum_i \tilde D_i^2(\tilde Y_i - \hat\theta\tilde D_i)^2}
{\big(\frac1n\sum_i \tilde D_i^2\big)^2}$$

::: {.check}
**Result:** $\sqrt n(\hat\theta - \theta_0) \to N(0,\sigma^2)$. Ordinary confidence intervals are
valid — despite black-box learners in the nuisance step. That is the whole point of the session.
:::

::: {.muted}
Repeat over several random splits and take the **median** of $\hat\theta$, to remove split
sensitivity.
:::

## Now do it on the real question

```{python}
#| echo: true
def dml_real(seed, K=5):
    n = len(Yr); ty, td = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
    for tr, te in KFold(K, shuffle=True, random_state=seed).split(Xr):
        ty[te] = Yr[te] - RandomForestRegressor(300, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0,
                                                n_jobs=-1).fit(Xr[tr], Yr[tr]).predict(Xr[te])
        td[te] = Dr[te] - RandomForestClassifier(300, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0,
                                                 n_jobs=-1).fit(Xr[tr], Dr[tr]).predict_proba(Xr[te])[:, 1]
    th = (td @ ty) / (td @ td)
    se = np.sqrt(np.mean(td**2 * (ty - th * td)**2)) / (np.mean(td**2) * np.sqrt(n))
    return th, se, ty, td

runs = [dml_real(s) for s in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)]
TH = float(np.median([r[0] for r in runs]))
SE = float(np.median([r[1] for r in runs]))
ols = sm.OLS(Yr, sm.add_constant(np.c_[Dr, Xr])).fit()

print(f"naive difference in means : {NAIVE:+6.2f}")
print(f"OLS, linear controls      : {ols.params[1]:+6.2f}  (se {ols.bse[1]:.2f})")
print(f"DML, cross-fitted forests : {TH:+6.2f}  (se {SE:.2f})"
      f"   95% CI [{TH-1.96*SE:+.2f}, {TH+1.96*SE:+.2f}]")
```

## The three answers, side by side

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.7, 2.95))

ax = axes[0]
est = [NAIVE, ols.params[1], TH]
errs = [0, 1.96 * ols.bse[1], 1.96 * SE]
names = ["naive\ndifference", "OLS with\nlinear controls", "DML with\ncross-fitting"]
cols = [CL.warn, CL.muted, CL.good]
ax.errorbar(est, range(3), xerr=errs, fmt="o", ms=8, lw=2.2,
            ecolor=CL.line, capsize=4, color="none",
            markerfacecolor="none", markeredgecolor="none")
for i, (e, er, c) in enumerate(zip(est, errs, cols)):
    ax.errorbar(e, i, xerr=er, fmt="o", ms=8, color=c, ecolor=c, capsize=4, lw=2.0)
ax.axvline(0, color=CL.ink, ls="--", lw=1.4)
ax.set_yticks(range(3)); ax.set_yticklabels(names, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("effect on digital intensity (points)")
ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)

ax = axes[1]
_, _, ty, td = runs[0]
ax.scatter(td, ty, s=13, color=CL.muted, alpha=.6, edgecolor="none")
xs = np.linspace(td.min(), td.max(), 50)
ax.plot(xs, TH * xs, color=CL.good, lw=2.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=CL.line, lw=1.0); ax.axvline(0, color=CL.line, lw=1.0)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\tilde D$ — treatment, residualised")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\tilde Y$ — outcome, residualised")
ax.set_title(f"slope = {TH:+.2f}", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
Ten points becomes **indistinguishable from zero**. The right-hand panel is the whole estimate: one
slope, through residualised data — Session 02's FWL picture, with forests doing the residualising.
:::

## Why the median over splits

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 2.5))
vals = [r[0] for r in runs]
ax.scatter(vals, [0] * len(vals), s=80, color=CL.accent, zorder=4)
ax.axvline(TH, color=CL.good, lw=2.2)
ax.text(TH, .18, f"median\n{TH:+.2f}", ha="center", color=CL.good, fontsize=9,
        fontweight="600")
ax.axvline(0, color=CL.ink, ls="--", lw=1.3)
ax.set_ylim(-.35, .45); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("estimate from each of five random fold assignments")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
The same data, the same code, five different random fold assignments — and estimates that differ by
more than a point. **Report the median across splits, and report the spread.**
:::

# 6 · Heterogeneous effects {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The question is often *for whom*

$$\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}\big[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x\big]$$

**Causal forests** (Wager & Athey) adapt random forests in three ways:

::: {.tight}
1. Splits maximise heterogeneity in the **treatment effect**, not in the outcome
2. **Honesty** — the observations that choose the splits are disjoint from those that estimate the
   leaf effects
3. The estimator is asymptotically normal and pointwise consistent, so **confidence intervals
   exist**
:::

::: {.muted}
Point 2 is Session 04's discipline again, moved inside the tree.
:::

## The discipline that must come with it

::: {.warn}
Searching over subgroups for large effects is **multiple testing**, and it will find something. With
twenty subgroups and a 5% test, one significant result is the *expected* outcome under no effect at
all.
:::

::: {.tight}
- **Pre-specify** subgroups wherever possible
- Otherwise report the **best linear projection** of $\hat\tau(X)$ on a small covariate set
- Or use a calibration test — the GATES / CLAN procedures of Chernozhukov et al.
- And label the whole section **exploratory**
:::

# 7 · What this does not fix {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Read this slide twice

::: {.warn}
DML delivers valid inference **conditional on the identifying assumptions**. If treatment is
confounded by something not in $X$, DML estimates a precisely-quantified **wrong number** — and its
narrow confidence interval will make the wrong number look authoritative.
:::

::: {.step}
Flexible nuisance estimation removes **functional-form error**. It does not remove
**omitted-variable bias**. Session 03's OVB formula still governs everything:

$$\hat\beta_{\text{short}} \to \beta_{\text{long}} + \gamma\,\delta$$
:::

## Which means the hard part is not the code

::: {.tight}
- The code is thirty lines and you have just read all of them
- The **argument** — why $X$ contains everything that drives both $D$ and $Y$ — is the paper
- That argument is made with institutional knowledge, not with cross-validation
:::

::: {.check}
On our own example, 41% of observations failed the overlap check. That fact belongs in the abstract,
not in a footnote.
:::

# Takeaways {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Key takeaways

::: {.tight}
1. Prediction accuracy and causal validity are **different properties**. One does not imply the other
2. The naive plug-in has two biases: regularisation ($b$) and overfitting ($c$)
3. An **orthogonal score** kills $b$ — errors in the nuisance become second-order
4. **Cross-fitting** kills $c$ — never evaluate a fit on its own training rows
5. Two $n^{-1/4}$ rates multiply into $n^{-1/2}$. Hence *double*
6. Heterogeneity searching is multiple testing. Pre-specify or label it exploratory
7. None of this identifies anything. **The assumptions do that**
:::

## What loses marks

::: {.tight}
- Reporting a DML estimate with **no overlap diagnostic**
- Fitting nuisances on the full sample (that is the naive plug-in, with extra steps)
- Reporting one fold assignment instead of the median over several
- Presenting a subgroup effect found by searching, without saying you searched
- Any sentence of the form "the model shows that $X$ causes $Y$"
:::

## Now, the practice

::: {.get}
Ninety minutes, in your groups. You will estimate one treatment effect three ways — naive, linear
controls, and cross-fitted DML — check overlap first, and write the paragraph defending conditional
ignorability. That paragraph carries the marks.
:::
